title: #70: Do you have a great business idea? Andreas Arni and Credit Suisse will back you up!
description: In the latest episode of the #StartupShow, we are visiting the Global HQ of Credit Suisse!  We had the pleasure to talk to Andreas Arni, Head of Entrepreneurs & Executives (E&E) at Credit Suisse Switzerland!  Andreas is passionate about collaborating with fresh entrepreneurs and he works closely with startups each and every day. With his extensive  experience in consulting and private banking, he invests his know-how in each of his clients.    Credit Suisse brings startups together with their experienced network in order to provide everything for a successful start: expertise, financial advice and support, and technical knowledge. As Andreas says: “When you make certain mistakes at the beginning, it's very difficult to correct them at a later stage.”  Website: https://www.credit-suisse.com  Enjoy the show!  Skip to Questions:  1:23 Who is Andreas Arni? 1:58 What makes you so passionate about working with entrepreneurs? 4:32 What are the main financial mistakes that entrepreneurs make in the early days of their venture? 5:54 In your opinion, what are the core strengths of Swiss entrepreneurs? 6:44 What do you think are the main disruptive industries that will come out of Switzerland? 7:47 When should a startup reach out to and bank such as Credit Suisse? 8:35 What is the difference between startup and corporate culture?  This is not an advertisement nor did anyone pay for this video in any way as per the day of publication 15.5.2017. All opinions are Cédric's or Andreas' and are approved by the communication department of Credit Suisse. —————————————— Cédric Bollag is an aspiring venture capitalist. Cédric decided to turn his passion about “Startups, Tech & Innovation” into a blog. He releases video interviews with entrepreneurs, investors and thought leaders in innovation. For any questions, suggestions and inquiries feel free to connect and reach out.  Connect with me on other social media channels: Cédric Bollag (Blogger & Founder): Email: [EMAIL] Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/cedric.bollag/ Snapchat: https://www.snapchat.com/add/cedric.bollag Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/cedric.bollag/ LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/cedricbollag/  GlobalTechBox.com: Instagram: https://instagram.com/globaltechbox/ Snapchat: https://www.snapchat.com/add/globaltechbox Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/globaltechbox/  Thank you for your attention!

asr.full_text: welcome to a new episode of the startup show today we are here at the global headquarters of Credit Suisse and I'm very excited to meet with Andres Arni who is the head of entrepreneurs and executives at Credit Suisse Switzerland welcome to the show Thank You Cedric for having me today it's a great pleasure to be on the show welcome back to a new episode of The Startup Show! Today you are here in Zurich, the global headquarters of Credit Suisse. It's a big pleasure, the first big bang here on The Startup Show which is really cool, I'm really excited about this. So Andreas, you know as usual on The Startup Show you get two minutes to introduce yourself to my audience. That's really great. Thank you for having me today here, it's a great honor, a great pleasure. I work for Cray Suisse. I work with entrepreneurs in Switzerland and my passion is really to help entrepreneurs to excel starting at the very early stage, you know talking about funding, financing, getting the company up and running and I think that's what we do and we've been very successful in the most recent years because we have a lot of start-up companies here in Switzerland, Swiss people but also global people coming to Switzerland and really getting started with their business here with us. But maybe you can give us a little bit of background about yourself, like where you're coming from I'm sure you have lucky I saw your LinkedIn you have some career path already behind you, tell us what brought you to this position here. I started out you know as a student in business yeah i was in consulting first and then i moved to banking and private banking particularly i worked a little bit abroad in latin america i came back to switzerland because i discovered my passion for you know entrepreneurs i have a business background i work with engineers i work with people in life science, and it's really an exciting job and I really love to do it every day. Right. So, so as you said, like your passion for, for start-ups, maybe you can pin-point a little bit like what exactly like that feeling is that you feel towards them? And like what makes it so exciting to work with, with entrepreneurs? At the beginning it's always just an idea. Sometimes people who have been studying with an idea for years but they don't know really how to get it on the ground. And then they come to us. And then we help them, to get structure, to get financing, to get advice by other experts. And what we really do in essence, is we bring together experienced entrepreneurs with startup people, people who want to fund the business. And we bring expertise. We bring financial means. And we also bring some technical know-how. For example, how to have your employees share in the business, how to structure yourself, how to write a business plan, and so on and so forth. It's really interesting, because first time I came across your name like I was surprised that Credit Suisse is offering some kind of service than what you are offering at the moment because when you associate a bank it it's usually you think about money, and you deposit your money. But this is totally a new way for the bank, bringing itself into startups. So maybe since you mentioned people, financing, how do you do that on a day-to-day basis? Well, Credit Suisse has, in its so to speak, entrepreneurship because Credit Suisse is founded by Alfred Escher, who was really one of the great entrepreneurs of Switzerland. You know, to building the railway system and everything. For a number of years now we have pursued this strategy which is called Bank for Entrepreneurs. Which caters to both like family enterprises in a later stage, which are dealing for example with succession issues, but also younger entrepreneurs who are growing. Switzerland, as a market, of course, it's way too small for a growth enterprise to really build itself out. So it's really about growing out of a small country into a global franchise. And that requires a lot of financial infrastructure. Yeah. So it's, you know, it's like about payments. It's about, you know about how to get credit, how to invest in expanding your business abroad, how to attract new talent, how to build in the talent in your franchise, how to incentivize this talent and that's so much of questions which are not maybe the traditional remit of banking, which is giving loans to businesses. But that's where we invest in our franchise because we want to grow. And Switzerland, as you can imagine it from a banking point of view, it's pretty saturated market. So we try to invest in the segment of young growth entrepreneurs because that's the future of our business, as well. You meet with a lot of entrepreneurs. You see a lot of startups. When you look at the financial points of a startup, what are mainly let's say the mistakes entrepreneurs do in the early days of their venture? Well, the people we work with, they typically come out of university, let's say in Zurich or Basel or Geneva or other places. And the people we work with are not essentially educated in financial matters. So as I said, they are mainly engineers or life science professionals. So we bring some ideas to them. You know, how to, as I said, write a business plan, and some people, they come to us in a very unstructured way. And we have to say, okay, but. first of all, you need to determine what kind of investments you need to do, how much money you want to get, how you want to attract investors without diluting yourself too much. And that's one of the big issues that we see. People who require capital in order to build a business, they want to maintain the control over the business, but at the same time, they are depending on outside investors. And how you actually balance this, you know, gaining or or attracting investors but at the same time not losing control over your enterprise that's one of the key questions that we see and it's a tricky one. Again I want to touch on your expertise with like meeting a lot of entrepreneurs maybe what are the core strengths when you look at the Swiss entrepreneurs when you see you window-building and like before we discussed a little bit briefly about like the mistakes they do but maybe you can also give us a little bit of and like your insights in terms of like the see when you're building? Before, we discussed briefly the mistakes they do, but maybe could you give us some insights into strength, the core competencies for the Swiss entrepreneur. I would say it has a lot to do with Switzerland as a place to do business. We have a lot of foreign entrepreneurs who come to Switzerland just to build up their business. It's because it's a very stable country, it's because our currency is strong, cost of funding are nowhere as low as in Switzerland. I would say specifically at the moment, where we have the negative interest rates from the central bank. And then, of course, it's access to talent. We have great educational system in Switzerland. There's a continuous flow of fresh talent coming out of the universities, out of the schools, which are available to the entrepreneurs. And if you ask any of the international people who came here to build out a business, they can certainly confirm that. You see again a lot of startups. What do you think are, let's say, some of the main industries, or disruptive industries that will come out from Switzerland? Switzerland is very strong traditionally and historically in life science and medtech. with Actelion selling itself to Johnson & Johnson. So it's a really big pool of talent out there. Then the second area, I would say it's e-commerce, FinTech and the likes, which you find mainly in the greater Zurich area, where we also have a big hub of expertise because we have Google here in Zurich and some other big e-commerce companies. And then you have a few smaller areas, which are also very important. For example, in the Western part of Switzerland, Geneva and the likes, we see see a new a fresh industry emerging out of the traditional watchmaking industry and its suppliers and the watchmakers today they are branching out they are diversifying more into the area of medical technology at what stage do you think like a startup who is just about to start should approach and come to a bank like yours? I would say it's never too early. When you have the idea, when you know what to do, call us and come to us and we will help you. We work together with a few great facilitators. These are companies which help startup companies to structure themselves and we do events with them together. We help them to find funding, we help them to have the right structure in place. Because the structure emerges as the company grows and it's very important to not make any big mistake in the beginning because sometimes the whole story is pretty much path-dependent, it means when you make a mistake in the beginning it's very tough to correct it at a later stage. One last question to wrap it up because I realise that a lot of my audience are students because of my network and maybe you can say like what is the main difference that you see between startup's culture versus corporate culture? It is a whole different world. But I see the key difference would be probably that an entrepreneur is essentially a risque taker. He's taking a lot of risks but he's also seeing a lot of upside in the corporate culture it's slightly different because you're not supposed to be a risk taker you're sometimes more of an internal politician but at the end of the day I would say if you wanna be successful in both worlds you need some kind of entrepreneurial gene I need some kind of entrepreneurial flair and that's where both worlds I think come together again. Cool, I think that's a nice statement to end this show thank you very much for taking the time I really appreciate it. And thank you very much for tuning in everybody and I'll see you soon with a new episode of the Startup Show. Thank you very much and have a good day.

In the latest episode of the #StartupShow, we are visiting the Global HQ of Credit Suisse! We had the pleasure to talk to Andreas Arni, Head of Entrepreneurs & Executives (E&E) at Credit Suisse Switzerland! Andreas is passionate about collaborating with fresh entrepreneurs and he works closely with startups each and every day. With his extensive experience in consulting and private banking, he invests his know-how in each of his clients. Credit Suisse brings startups together with their experienced network in order to provide everything for a successful start: expertise, financial advice and support, and technical knowledge. As Andreas says: “When you make certain mistakes at the beginning, it's very difficult to correct them at a later stage.” Website: https://www.credit-suisse.com Enjoy the show! Skip to Questions: 1:23 Who is Andreas Arni? 1:58 What makes you so passionate about working with entrepreneurs? 4:32 What are the main financial mistakes that entrepreneurs make in the early days of their venture? 5:54 In your opinion, what are the core strengths of Swiss entrepreneurs? 6:44 What do you think are the main disruptive industries that will come out of Switzerland? 7:47 When should a startup reach out to and bank such as Credit Suisse? 8:35 What is the difference between startup and corporate culture? This is not an advertisement nor did anyone pay for this video in any way as per the day of publication 15.5.2017. All opinions are Cédric's or Andreas' and are approved by the communication department of Credit Suisse. —————————————— Cédric Bollag is an aspiring

venture capitalist. Cédric decided to turn his passion about “Startups, Tech & Innovation” into a blog. He releases video interviews with entrepreneurs, investors and thought leaders in innovation. For any questions, suggestions and inquiries feel free to connect and reach out. Connect with me on other social media channels: Cédric Bollag (Blogger & Founder): Email: [EMAIL] Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/cedric.bollag/ Snapchat: https://www.snapchat.com/add/cedric.bollag Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/cedric.bollag/ LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/cedricbollag/ GlobalTechBox.com: Instagram: https://instagram.com/globaltechbox/ Snapchat: https://www.snapchat.com/add/globaltechbox Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/globaltechbox/ Thank you for your attention!

welcome to a new episode of the startup show today we are here at the global headquarters of Credit Suisse and I'm very excited to meet with Andres Arni who is the head of entrepreneurs and executives at Credit Suisse Switzerland welcome to the show Thank You Cedric for having me today it's a great pleasure to be on the show welcome back to a new episode of The Startup Show! Today you are here in Zurich, the global headquarters of Credit Suisse. It's a big pleasure, the first big bang here on The Startup Show which is really cool, I'm really excited about this. So Andreas, you know as usual on The Startup Show you get two minutes to introduce yourself to my audience. That's really great. Thank you for having me today here, it's a great honor, a great pleasure. I work for Cray Suisse. I work with entrepreneurs in Switzerland and my passion is really to help entrepreneurs to excel starting at the very early stage, you know talking about funding, financing, getting the company up and running and I think that's what we do and we've been very successful in the most recent years because we have a lot of start-up companies here in Switzerland, Swiss people but also global people coming to Switzerland and really getting started with their business here with us. But maybe you can give us a little bit of background about yourself, like where you're coming from I'm sure you have lucky I saw your LinkedIn you have some career path already behind you, tell us what brought you to this position here. I started out you know as a student in business yeah i was in consulting first and then

i moved to banking and private banking particularly i worked a little bit abroad in latin america i came back to switzerland because i discovered my passion for you know entrepreneurs i have a business background i work with engineers i work with people in life science, and it's really an exciting job and I really love to do it every day. Right. So, so as you said, like your passion for, for start-ups, maybe you can pin-point a little bit like what exactly like that feeling is that you feel towards them? And like what makes it so exciting to work with, with entrepreneurs? At the beginning it's always just an idea. Sometimes people who have been studying with an idea for years but they don't know really how to get it on the ground. And then they come to us. And then we help them, to get structure, to get financing, to get advice by other experts. And what we really do in essence, is we bring together experienced entrepreneurs with startup people, people who want to fund the business. And we bring expertise. We bring financial means. And we also bring some technical know-how. For example, how to have your employees share in the business, how to structure yourself, how to write a business plan, and so on and so forth. It's really interesting, because first time I came across your name like I was surprised that Credit Suisse is offering some kind of service than what you are offering at the moment because when you associate a bank it it's usually you think about money, and you deposit your money. But this is totally a new way for the bank, bringing itself into startups. So

maybe since you mentioned people, financing, how do you do that on a day-to-day basis? Well, Credit Suisse has, in its so to speak, entrepreneurship because Credit Suisse is founded by Alfred Escher, who was really one of the great entrepreneurs of Switzerland. You know, to building the railway system and everything. For a number of years now we have pursued this strategy which is called Bank for Entrepreneurs. Which caters to both like family enterprises in a later stage, which are dealing for example with succession issues, but also younger entrepreneurs who are growing. Switzerland, as a market, of course, it's way too small for a growth enterprise to really build itself out. So it's really about growing out of a small country into a global franchise. And that requires a lot of financial infrastructure. Yeah. So it's, you know, it's like about payments. It's about, you know about how to get credit, how to invest in expanding your business abroad, how to attract new talent, how to build in the talent in your franchise, how to incentivize this talent and that's so much of questions which are not maybe the traditional remit of banking, which is giving loans to businesses. But that's where we invest in our franchise because we want to grow. And Switzerland, as you can imagine it from a banking point of view, it's pretty saturated market. So we try to invest in the segment of young growth entrepreneurs because that's the future of our business, as well. You meet with a lot of entrepreneurs. You see a lot of startups. When you look at the financial points of a startup, what

are mainly let's say the mistakes entrepreneurs do in the early days of their venture? Well, the people we work with, they typically come out of university, let's say in Zurich or Basel or Geneva or other places. And the people we work with are not essentially educated in financial matters. So as I said, they are mainly engineers or life science professionals. So we bring some ideas to them. You know, how to, as I said, write a business plan, and some people, they come to us in a very unstructured way. And we have to say, okay, but. first of all, you need to determine what kind of investments you need to do, how much money you want to get, how you want to attract investors without diluting yourself too much. And that's one of the big issues that we see. People who require capital in order to build a business, they want to maintain the control over the business, but at the same time, they are depending on outside investors. And how you actually balance this, you know, gaining or or attracting investors but at the same time not losing control over your enterprise that's one of the key questions that we see and it's a tricky one. Again I want to touch on your expertise with like meeting a lot of entrepreneurs maybe what are the core strengths when you look at the Swiss entrepreneurs when you see you window-building and like before we discussed a little bit briefly about like the mistakes they do but maybe you can also give us a little bit of and like your insights in terms of like the see when you're building? Before, we discussed briefly the mistakes they do, but maybe

could you give us some insights into strength, the core competencies for the Swiss entrepreneur. I would say it has a lot to do with Switzerland as a place to do business. We have a lot of foreign entrepreneurs who come to Switzerland just to build up their business. It's because it's a very stable country, it's because our currency is strong, cost of funding are nowhere as low as in Switzerland. I would say specifically at the moment, where we have the negative interest rates from the central bank. And then, of course, it's access to talent. We have great educational system in Switzerland. There's a continuous flow of fresh talent coming out of the universities, out of the schools, which are available to the entrepreneurs. And if you ask any of the international people who came here to build out a business, they can certainly confirm that. You see again a lot of startups. What do you think are, let's say, some of the main industries, or disruptive industries that will come out from Switzerland? Switzerland is very strong traditionally and historically in life science and medtech. with Actelion selling itself to Johnson & Johnson. So it's a really big pool of talent out there. Then the second area, I would say it's e-commerce, FinTech and the likes, which you find mainly in the greater Zurich area, where we also have a big hub of expertise because we have Google here in Zurich and some other big e-commerce companies. And then you have a few smaller areas, which are also very important. For example, in the Western part of Switzerland, Geneva and the likes, we see see a new

a fresh industry emerging out of the traditional watchmaking industry and its suppliers and the watchmakers today they are branching out they are diversifying more into the area of medical technology at what stage do you think like a startup who is just about to start should approach and come to a bank like yours? I would say it's never too early. When you have the idea, when you know what to do, call us and come to us and we will help you. We work together with a few great facilitators. These are companies which help startup companies to structure themselves and we do events with them together. We help them to find funding, we help them to have the right structure in place. Because the structure emerges as the company grows and it's very important to not make any big mistake in the beginning because sometimes the whole story is pretty much path-dependent, it means when you make a mistake in the beginning it's very tough to correct it at a later stage. One last question to wrap it up because I realise that a lot of my audience are students because of my network and maybe you can say like what is the main difference that you see between startup's culture versus corporate culture? It is a whole different world. But I see the key difference would be probably that an entrepreneur is essentially a risque taker. He's taking a lot of risks but he's also seeing a lot of upside in the corporate culture it's slightly different because you're not supposed to be a risk taker you're sometimes more of an internal politician but at the end of the day I would say if you wanna be

successful in both worlds you need some kind of entrepreneurial gene I need some kind of entrepreneurial flair and that's where both worlds I think come together again. Cool, I think that's a nice statement to end this show thank you very much for taking the time I really appreciate it. And thank you very much for tuning in everybody and I'll see you soon with a new episode of the Startup Show. Thank you very much and have a good day.
